topic.name: Prenatal Care
objectives: Schedule prenatal visits and perform appropriate screenings at each gestational age
Interpret routine prenatal labs and identify abnormal values requiring intervention
Diagnose and manage common pregnancy complaints (N/V, GERD, back pain, edema)
Identify high-risk conditions requiring referral or escalation of care

lessons.title: 📅 Prenatal Visit Schedule: What and When

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Danielle, 28, G1P0, missed her first prenatal visit until 18 weeks because 'I didn't know I was supposed to go that early.' She missed first-trimester screening, the NT ultrasound window closed, and she ended up needing CVS instead of NIPT for reassurance. Then at 28 weeks, she came in with a headache and blurry vision — PIH was missed because her BP wasn't checked regularly. The prenatal visit schedule isn't arbitrary; every visit has a purpose, and missing windows has real consequences. As an FNP, you'll be the one managing most prenatal care until delivery.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Pregnancy timeline from conception to 40 weeks with markers showing when each screening/test occurs

content_chunks.title: Prenatal Visit Schedule (ACOG Guidelines)
content_chunks.content:
**Standard Schedule for Uncomplicated Pregnancy**:

| Gestation | Visit Frequency | Key Deliverables |
|---|---|---|
| **<28 wk** | Every 4 weeks | Establish dating, baseline labs, nuchal translucency, anatomy scan |
| **28-36 wk** | Every 2 weeks | GDM screening, Rhogam (28 wk), Tdap (27-36 wk), growth scan |
| **36 wk to delivery** | Weekly | Group B Strep screen, cervical checks (optional), presentation, fetal movement counts |

**First Visit (8-12 wk)** — The BIG one:
✅ Confirm pregnancy (urine/blood hCG, viability US)
✅ **Dating ultrasound** (most accurate 8-12 wk — CRL)
✅ Complete history: LMP, prior pregnancies, medical/surgical, meds, family/genetic
✅ **Standard labs**: CBC, blood type + Rh, antibody screen, rubella IgG, VDRL/RPR, HBsAg, HIV, varicella IgG, pap, urine culture
✅ NIPT (cfDNA) for aneuploidy screening — offered to ALL, recommended age ≥35
✅ Nuchal translucency US (11-13.6 wk)
✅ Counseling: Nutrition (prenatal vitamins!), exercise, medication safety, red flags

**18-22 Week Visit**: **Anatomy scan** — fetal survey, placental location, cervical length
content_chunks.mnemonic: **FIRST AID for first visit**: **F**undal height, **I**mmunizations/rubella, **R**h type, **S**TIs (HIV, RPR, hep B), **T**SH, **A**neuploidy screening, **I**ron stores (CBC), **D**ating ultrasound
content_chunks.visual_desc: Calendar-style graphic showing pregnancy divided into trimesters with visit frequency icons and key screening milestones

content_chunks.title: Screening Tests — When & Why
content_chunks.content:
**First Trimester**:
• **NIPT (cfDNA)**: Screens for trisomies 21, 18, 13 — sensitivity >99% for T21. Can detect sex chromosome abnormalities.
• **NT Ultrasound**: Nuchal translucency ≥3.5mm → higher risk of aneuploidy + structural heart defects
• **Carrier screening**: Cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, hemoglobinopathies — ideally prior to or early in pregnancy

**Second Trimester**:
• **Maternal serum AFP (quad screen)**: Open neural tube defects (ONTDs), ventral wall defects, multiple gestation. Done 16-18 wk (making way to cfDNA but still used when NIPT unavailable)
• **Anatomy scan (18-22 wk)**: Detailed fetal anatomy survey; if cervical length <25mm → short cervix, Tocolysis + progesterone

**24-28 Weeks**:
• **1-hour Glucose Challenge Test (GCT)**: 50g glucose, check at 1 hour → ≥140 mg/dL = abnormal → proceed to 3-hour GTT
• **Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)**: 100g glucose, fasting + 1, 2, 3 hour levels
  - Carpenter-Coustan criteria: Fasting ≥95, 1h ≥180, 2h ≥155, 3h ≥140 (any 2 abnormal = GDM)

**36 Weeks**:
• **Group B Streptococcus (GBS)**: Vaginal-rectal swab → if positive, intrapartum penicillin

**If Rh negative**: **Rhogam (RhoGAM)** at 28 wk AND within 72 hours of any bleeding, trauma, amniocentesis, or delivery
content_chunks.visual_desc: Timeline infographic with gestational weeks on x-axis and screening tests shown as icons placed at their appropriate timing windows

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Don't miss Tdap in EVERY pregnancy!** Tdap (27-36 wk) provides passive immunity to newborn against pertussis. Does NOT matter when last Tdap was — give in EVERY pregnancy regardless of prior vaccination interval. Also: **COVID-19 and flu vaccines are SAFE in any trimester**. Recommend them.

quick_checks.q: A G1P0 patient at 12 weeks comes for her first visit. Which of the following is NOT typically done at this visit?
quick_checks.explanation: GBS screening is done at 36 weeks. First visit includes dating US, NIPT offer, and standard prenatal labs.

quick_checks.q: When should Tdap vaccine be given during pregnancy?
answers: Only if the patient hasn't had Tdap in 10 years
quick_checks.explanation: Tdap is recommended at 27-36 weeks EVERY pregnancy regardless of prior vaccination interval, to maximize passive antibody transfer to newborn.

lessons.title: 🤢 Common Pregnancy Complaints: What's Normal, What's Not

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Tara, 26, G3P2, is 8 weeks pregnant and 'can't keep anything down.' She's lost 8 pounds in 2 weeks, has ketones in her urine, and her husband is terrified. She's been told 'morning sickness is normal' but she's vomited 6 times today. This is hyperemesis gravidarum — not 'normal' morning sickness — and she needs treatment. On the other end of the spectrum, Emily, 34 weeks, is worried about swelling in her ankles and hands. Is it normal edema or preeclampsia? Differentiating routine discomfort from dangerous complications is the skill that separates a good FNP from a great one.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Split illustration: Left side shows mild symptoms (normal pregnancy), right side shows red-flag symptoms requiring urgent evaluation

content_chunks.title: Nausea & Vomiting of Pregnancy vs. Hyperemesis Gravidarum
content_chunks.content:
**Nausea & Vomiting of Pregnancy (NVP)** — 'Morning sickness':
• 70-80% of pregnancies, peaks at 9 weeks, resolves by 16-20 weeks
• Mild to moderate, doesn't cause significant dehydration or weight loss
• **Treatment**: Dietary changes (small frequent meals, bland foods, ginger 250mg QID, vitamin B6 10-25mg TID)

**Hyperemesis Gravidarum (HG)** — Severe form:
• **Persistent vomiting** causing:
  - >5% weight loss from pre-pregnancy weight
  - Dehydration + ketonuria
  - Electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis)
  - Nutritional deficiencies (thiamine!) → risk of Wernicke encephalopathy
• **Treatment**:
  1. **First-line**: Doxylamine 12.5mg + Pyridoxine 25mg TID (Diclegis/Bonjesta — FDA-approved!)
  2. **Second-line**: Ondansetron (Zofran) — caution: debate about cleft palate risk, benefit usually outweighs risk
  3. **Third-line**: Metoclopramide, promethazine, or prochlorperazine
  4. **Refractory**: IV fluids + electrolyte repletion, TPN if severe, steroids (last resort)
  - Always give **thiamine (B1)** before IV dextrose to prevent Wernicke's!

**Warning Signs requiring evaluation**: Weight loss >5%, ketonuria, inability to keep fluids down 24+ hours, abdominal pain, fever
content_chunks.visual_desc: Comparison table contrasting NVP (mild, self-limited) with HG (severe, weight loss, dehydration, needs treatment)

content_chunks.title: Other Common Complaints & Management
content_chunks.content:
**GERD / Heartburn** (30-50% of pregnancies):
• **Mechanism**: Progesterone relaxes LES + enlarging uterus increases intra-abdominal pressure
• **Treatment**: Antacids (calcium carbonate, Tums), H2 blockers (ranitidine/famotidine — safe!), PPIs (omeprazole — safe!)
• **Lifestyle**: Small meals, avoid lying flat after eating, elevate head of bed

**Low Back Pain** (50-80%):
• **Mechanism**: Relaxin + lordosis from growing belly
• **Treatment**: PT, acetaminophen (AVOID NSAIDs/ibuprofen!), maternity support belt, warm compresses
• **Red flag**: Back pain + fever + dysuria = pyelonephritis! Get urinalysis

**Edema** (legs, feet, hands):
• **Normal**: Dependent edema, worse at day's end, improves with elevation, no other symptoms
• **ABNORMAL (worrisome)**: Sudden onset, facial/hand edema, +HTN, +proteinuria → **pre-eclampsia!**
• **Management**: Elevation, compression stockings, avoid prolonged standing, hydration

**Round Ligament Pain** (sharp groin pain with movement):
• **Reassurance** — normal stretching! Sudden movement triggers brief sharp pain
• Red flag if pain is constant, fever, vomiting, or accompanied by vaginal bleeding

**Shortness of Breath**:
• **Normal**: Progesterone increases respiratory drive, enlarged uterus → decreased lung volume
• **ABNORMAL**: Sudden onset, pleuritic, with chest pain, or with unilateral leg swelling → PE risk (pregnancy is hypercoagulable!)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Body diagram showing a pregnant silhouette with numbered areas: 1. Head (HA → preeclampsia), 2. Chest (SOB → PE?), 3. Upper abdomen (GERD), 4. Lower back, 5. Legs (edema, DVT)

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Medication safety in pregnancy simplified**: Tylenol (acetaminophen) = safe. Ibuprofen/NSAIDs = AVOID (risk of oligohydramnios, premature ductus arteriosus closure — especially after 20 wk). Most antibiotics = safe (penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides except erythromycin estolate). DOXYCYCLINE and TETRACYCLINE = contraindicated (bone/tooth effects). **Levothyroxine doses often need to INCREASE by 30-50% in pregnancy** — check TSH every 4 weeks!

quick_checks.q: A patient at 10 weeks has lost 7% of her pre-pregnancy weight, has ketones in urine, and vomits 5+ times daily. What is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
quick_checks.explanation: Weight loss >5%, ketonuria, and persistent vomiting despite conservative measures = hyperemesis gravidarum. First-line treatment is doxylamine + pyridoxine (Diclegis).

quick_checks.q: Which of the following symptoms in a 34-week pregnant patient requires immediate evaluation?
answers: Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Sharp groin pain with sudden movement
New onset facial edema with headache and visual changes
quick_checks.explanation: Facial edema + headache + visual changes = preeclampsia until proven otherwise. Check BP and urine protein. The other options are common, benign pregnancy complaints.

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Keisha, 32, G2P1, has a history of C-section. She's now 39 weeks and feels a 'tearing' sensation in her lower abdomen. She had an appointment tomorrow but didn't think this was urgent. Her husband insisted she come in. Her vitals are stable, but her abdomen is tender over the previous C-section scar, and FHR tracing shows variable decelerations. Uterine rupture is a life-threatening emergency. Recognizing high-risk conditions and knowing when to refer — or when to send straight to the ER — is critical for safe FNP practice.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Warning sign icons: pregnant silhouette with red exclamation points at critical areas (abdomen, head, chest, legs)

content_chunks.title: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
content_chunks.content:
**Classification** (ACOG):

| Condition | BP | Proteinuria | Other Features |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chronic HTN** | ≥140/90 before 20 wk | ± | Preexisting |
| **Gestational HTN** | ≥140/90 after 20 wk | Negative | No systemic features |
| **Preeclampsia** | ≥140/90 after 20 wk | ≥300mg/24h or ≥1+ dipstick | May have end-organ dysfunction |
| **Eclampsia** | ≥140/90 | ± | +Seizures |
| **HELLP** | ± | ± | Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets |

**Preeclampsia Warning Signs (CRUSH)**:
• **C**loudy vision / **C**onfusion
• **R**ight upper quadrant pain (liver capsule distension)
• **U**rine output decreased
• **S**evere headache
• **H**ypertension + edema

**Crescendo pattern**: Gestational HTN → mild preeclampsia → severe preeclampsia → eclampsia → HELLP

**Prevention**: Low-dose aspirin 81mg daily starting at 12-16 wk for HIGH-RISK patients (prior preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, CKD, DM, chronic HTN, autoimmune disease)

**Treatment**: Delivery is the only cure! Mild: manage outpatient with BP control. Severe: admit, give magnesium for seizure prophylaxis, deliver.

**Postpartum**: Risk persists for 6-12 weeks postpartum. BP can worsen at 3-6 days postpartum (fluid mobilization)!
content_chunks.mnemonic: **CRUSH** for preeclampsia warning signs: **C**loudy vision, **R**UQ pain, **U**rine output down, **S**evere HA, **H**TN
content_chunks.visual_desc: Staircase diagram showing progression from chronic/gestational HTN → preeclampsia → severe preeclampsia → eclampsia → HELLP with defining features at each step

content_chunks.title: Red Flags That Need Immediate Referral/ER
content_chunks.content:
**OB Emergencies — Don't Miss These**:

🚨 **Preeclampsia with Severe Features**:
• BP ≥160/110 (confirmed in 15 min)
• Severe headache, visual changes, RUQ pain
• Pulmonary edema
• Platelets <100K, Cr >1.1, AST/ALT >2× normal
→ **Call OB!** Likely need admission, magnesium, delivery

🚨 **Eclampsia**: Seizure + HTN/proteinuria → ABCs, magnesium 4-6g IV, emergency C-section

🚨 **Vaginal Bleeding in 3rd Trimester**:
• **Placenta previa** (painless bright red bleeding) — NO vaginal exam! STAT ultrasound
• **Placental abruption** (painful dark bleeding + rigid/firm uterus) — fetal distress → C-section

🚨 **PPROM (Preterm Premature Rupture of Membranes)**:
• Gush of fluid + pooling on speculum exam + positive ferning/nitrazine
• <37 weeks → steroids for fetal lung maturity, antibiotics (group B strep coverage), monitor for chorioamnionitis

🚨 **Decreased Fetal Movement**:
• <10 movements in 2 hours in 3rd trimester
• Kick counts: Should feel ≥10 kicks in 2 hours after a meal
• → NST (non-stress test) + BPP (biophysical profile)

🚨 **VTE / DVT / PE in Pregnancy**:
• Unilateral leg swelling/pain, chest pain, SOB
• Pregnancy is 5× higher VTE risk (hypercoagulable state!)
• Workup: venous Doppler, CT pulmonary angiogram or V/Q scan
• Treatment: LMWH (enoxaparin) — NOT warfarin (teratogenic)

🚨 **Postpartum Red Flags**:
• Hemorrhage (>500mL vag delivery, >1000mL C-section)
• Endometritis (fever + fundal tenderness + foul lochia)
• Postpartum preeclampsia (can occur up to 6 weeks after delivery!)
content_chunks.visual_desc: ER-style triage board with each emergency listed as a case with symptoms, vitals, and action required

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Crash C-section readiness**: When you send a patient with suspected uterine rupture, placental abruption with fetal distress, or cord prolapse to the ER — call ahead and say: 'I'm sending a potentially crashing OB patient.' STAT page the OB team. Minutes matter. Also: **Magnesium is the drug for eclampsia prophylaxis**, NOT phenytoin or diazepam. Know the magnesium dosing: 4-6g IV loading over 15-20 min, then 2g/hr maintenance.

quick_checks.q: A G3P2 at 32 weeks presents with a painless gush of fluid and positive ferning on exam. What is the NEXT step?
answers: Admit for observation, give betamethasone × 2 doses
Reassure and send home with follow-up
Check NST and discharge if reassuring
quick_checks.explanation: PPROM <37 weeks → admit, give corticosteroids (betamethasone) for fetal lung maturity, monitor for chorioamnionitis, and plan delivery timing. Term PROM (≥37 wks) → induce.

quick_checks.q: Which of the following is a severe feature of preeclampsia requiring immediate delivery?
answers: BP 165/112 with headache and RUQ pain
quick_checks.explanation: BP ≥160/110 + severe headache + RUQ pain = preeclampsia with severe features. Needs immediate referral/admission for magnesium, BP control, and delivery planning.
